title: Early-life exposure to hardship increased risk tolerance and entrepreneurship in adulthood with gender differences.
ehr_evidence: The principal sources of information are 1) the 1990 Population Census (1% sample) for the population by county and year of birth used to estimate cohort losses; 2) the 2005 Population Mini-Census (20% sample) used to measure entrepreneurship; 3) the 2013 nationally representative CHFS for business ownership and risk tolerance; and 4) the China Meteorological Administration for daily instrumental temperature records at 727 stations between 1951 and 1970.
summary: A quasi-natural experiment exploiting China's Great Famine via census and household-survey data to test whether early-life hardship increases adult entrepreneurship and risk tolerance, with gender differences.
key_findings: In counties where the famine was one SD more severe, women and men were 17.1% and 12.7% more likely to engage in entrepreneurship (self-employed or business owner), with famine-intensity coefficients of 0.058 (SE 0.010) for women and 0.111 (SE 0.018) for men (P < 0.01).

Among male entrepreneurs, the famine-intensity coefficient on the log of monthly income was positive and significant and 1.7 times that among female entrepreneurs; among female entrepreneurs it was positive but not significant.
Hardship increased risk tolerance among both women and men: a one-SD higher famine intensity made women and men 18.4% and 13.2% more likely to be risk tolerant.

Among men only, both hardship and own risk tolerance increased business ownership, and the famine-intensity coefficient fell about 15% after controlling for risk tolerance, indicating partial mediation.
Male entrepreneurship increased with the wife's risk tolerance but not vice versa, consistent with intrahousehold risk pooling.
Self-confidence, tenacity, resilience, and opportunism were not significant in the direction that would increase entrepreneurship.
captured_features: entrepreneurship indicator (self-employed or business owner; narrow business ownership)
log of monthly income among entrepreneurs
individual controls (age, ethnicity, education, rural residence, health status)
study_design: quasi-natural experiment (cohort exploiting the Great Famine with region fixed effects)
population: Chinese adults born before 1962 exposed during the Great Famine (1959-1961); 729,401 persons in 2,589 counties (2005 Mini-Census) and 12,188 persons in 167 counties (2013 CHFS)
limitations: Analysis relied on risk tolerance as a proxy for ambiguity tolerance rather than measuring ambiguity directly.

Individual-level estimates combined selective mortality and operant conditioning, potentially overestimating the conditioning effect, and county-level estimates could not fully separate the two mechanisms.
The CHFS surveyed risk tolerance of only one spouse, preventing estimation of an equation with both own and spouse risk tolerance.
Exposure and outcomes were based on census and self-reported survey data rather than clinical or health records.
